judgments.yea_description: Voted to widen Wyoming's prostitution law to cover sexual touching, not just sexual intrusion. Wyoming's prostitution law covered only sexual intrusion. The act adds sexual contact. That means touching another person's intimate parts, or having them touch yours, for sexual arousal, gratification or abuse. The same words are added to the crime of soliciting an act of prostitution. The penalties do not change. Each stays a misdemeanor carrying up to six months in jail, a fine of up to $750, or both. Every county sheriff must report to a legislative committee each year on convictions under the two crimes. The report must also name any massage business that closed because of charges or convictions under the act. The Senate passed the bill 17-14 and it became law as chapter 163 of the 2025 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to fund Wyoming's 2025 water projects and add $80 million to two large dam and canal rebuilds. The act is Wyoming's 2025 water construction bill. It authorizes 18 new water projects and puts $21.5 million behind them. The work ranges from town water tanks and transmission pipelines to irrigation canals, spillways and small stock-water systems. The state usually pays half a project's cost, and the sponsor must raise the rest. Seven of the projects also carry a state loan at 4% interest, over terms of twenty to thirty years. The act then adds $80 million to two large projects already under way. The state's share of the Goshen Irrigation District tunnels rises from $21.8 million to $41.8 million, and its share of the LaPrele dam rebuild rises from $30 million to $90 million. Both increases are drawn from the legislative stabilization reserve account. The act also moves $4.2 million between two water development accounts, pays for one new state engineer position, and puts $148,000 into updating how the state measures the North Platte River's flow. The House agreed to the Senate changes 34-26 and the bill became law as chapter 111 of the 2025 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to let the state regulate oil and gas waste pits wherever they sit, not just on a lease. Oil and gas drilling leaves pits that hold drilling fluid, produced water and emergency overflow waste. The Oil and Gas Conservation Commission regulates those pits so they do not foul state waters. Until this act, that power reached only pits sitting on a lease, unit or shared drilling area. The act strikes those words. The commission may now set rules for where such a pit goes, how it is built, how it is run and how it is cleaned up, wherever it sits. Discharges already covered by the federal clean water permit stay outside its reach. The Senate passed the bill 23-7 and it became law as chapter 17 of the 2025 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to require the state to notify Wyoming's tribal governments about nearby industrial projects. Anyone who wants to build a large industrial plant in Wyoming needs a state siting permit. Local governments have long been told when such an application arrives. The act gives tribal governments the same standing. It names the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribal governments and the joint tribal governing body of the Wind River Indian Reservation. When a proposed plant is in their county or the next one over, the state must give them notice of the application, or of a request to skip it. The state must also send them a copy of the application and tell them about the meetings and hearings that follow. The rule covers applications filed on or after July 1, 2025. The Senate passed the bill 17-13 and it became law as chapter 18 of the 2025 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to let adult students keep the Wyoming's Tomorrow scholarship after a break in enrollment. Wyoming's Tomorrow scholarship helps adult students pay for community college. To keep it, a student had to stay continuously enrolled. The act repeals that requirement. A student who steps away for a term and comes back no longer loses the scholarship for that reason alone. Nothing else about the program changes. The House passed the bill 36-25 and it became law as chapter 31 of the 2026 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to let struggling county hospitals file for bankruptcy instead of closing. A county hospital or hospital district in money trouble had one path in state law: dissolve and close. The act adds a second. Trustees may now vote to file for city and county bankruptcy under chapter 9 of the federal code, and work out a plan to pay down the debt. For a county hospital, the county commissioners must first approve the filing and the first debt plan. For a hospital district, no public vote is needed. Instead the filing and plan must go up on the district's website at least seven days before the trustees meet on it. The House passed the bill 38-21 and it became law as chapter 13 of the 2026 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to make it a separate crime to cross county or state lines to evade police or continue a crime. The act creates a new crime called absconding for criminal purposes. A person commits it by traveling from one Wyoming county to another, or out of the state, in any of three situations. The first is having committed a crime under Wyoming's criminal code or its controlled substances law, and traveling to evade or elude police. The second is traveling with intent to commit another such crime after already committing one in the first county. The third is traveling to get rid of or hide the proceeds or property from such a crime. The penalty is not fixed. It matches the penalty for the most serious crime that was committed, meant to be committed, or furthered by the travel. The Senate passed the bill 17-13 and it became law as chapter 12 of the 2026 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to make the Wyoming Indian Child Welfare Act permanent instead of letting it expire. The Wyoming Indian Child Welfare Act sets the rules state courts follow in child custody cases involving Native American children. The act was written to expire on July 1, 2026. This law repeals that expiry date. The Wyoming Indian Child Welfare Act now stays in force with no end date, and the legislature does not have to renew it. The House passed the bill 40-20 and it became law as chapter 57 of the 2026 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to fund Wyoming's 2026 water projects and set a deadline on the Alkali Creek Reservoir. The act is Wyoming's 2026 water construction bill. It authorizes 24 water projects and puts $27.9 million behind them. The work runs from town wells, tanks and transmission pipelines to irrigation pipelines, diversions, siphons and small stock-water systems. The state usually pays half a project's cost and the sponsor raises the rest, though a few projects get all their materials paid for. Seven projects also carry a state loan at 4% interest, over terms of ten to forty years. Newcastle's grant is held back until the state agrees the town has allowed water sales outside city limits. The act moves $16.2 million between two water development accounts and hands a test well to the city of Douglas for at least $610,838. It also sets a hard stop on the Alkali Creek Reservoir project. No further time extensions are intended, and from January 1, 2027 its money may not be spent or used to take land by eminent domain. Two studies are funded: $155,000 to measure how forest management affects water yield, and a review of how small water project applications are handled. The Senate agreed to the House changes 21-10 and the bill became law as chapter 73 of the 2026 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to let private providers handle Wyoming driver's license tests and motor vehicle services. The act lets the transportation department hire outside firms to do driver's license and vehicle work. They may give the written, driving and skills tests and handle other vehicle services. The department may set up a partner program and decide which services those firms may offer. It must write rules on who qualifies, training, background checks, bonding, fees, monitoring, audits, and how a firm loses the work. The rules must keep the firms in line with federal standards for testing truck drivers. A firm doing this work is not a government body. The House passed the bill 39-21 and it became law as chapter 71 of the 2026 session laws.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to let Wyoming pharmacists assess patients and prescribe under board rules. The act writes a definition of the practice of pharmacy into Wyoming law. It covers reading, judging, mixing, handing out and giving medicines, and counseling patients. It also covers checking a patient in order to prescribe drugs and devices, and starting pharmacist care services, both under rules the board of pharmacy writes. Working with a doctor under a shared care agreement is part of the practice too. No pharmacist has to enter such an agreement, and an employer may not treat a pharmacist worse for refusing. The board of pharmacy must write the rules that make all of this work. The House passed the bill 41-20 and it became law as chapter 103 of the 2026 session laws.
